claims.text: Tribo-corrosion degradation in high-entropy alloys is governed by competition between mechanical passive-film removal and electrochemical repassivation.
When passive-film removal outpaces repair, both wear and corrosion accelerate.
The proposed alloy initially has a homogeneous microstructure.
The proposed alloy naturally forms a stable passive film.
Varying sliding load or speed and electrochemical potential can separately and jointly modulate passive-film removal and repassivation rates.
Simultaneous sliding in a chloride-rich electrolyte can be compared with inert sliding and static immersion to separate coupled degradation from isolated wear and corrosion.
Passive-film integrity and continuity are the structural mediator of the coupled response.
Film defects and mechanically induced grain-structure changes influence passive-film integrity.
Mechanical sliding disrupts the passive film and exposes the underlying metal to the corrosive environment.
The electrolyte simultaneously promotes reformation of the mechanically damaged film.
A film-removal rate exceeding the repassivation rate enhances localized corrosion by exposing vulnerable substrate areas.
The same removal–repair imbalance accelerates wear.

Increasing sliding load or speed without enhanced repassivation will increase total degradation and produce both higher wear rate and higher corrosion current density than isolated-wear or isolated-corrosion baselines.
More aggressive electrochemical conditions will increase coupled degradation when repassivation is not correspondingly enhanced.
Inert sliding preserves the passive film while isolating wear.
The prediction should hold where electrochemical conditions permit at least some passive-film reformation.
The prediction may fail or become less distinct at ultra-high sliding forces, at chloride concentrations that completely inhibit repassivation, or in alloys with non-homogeneous microstructures.
Alloy composition, microstructure, and environmental aggressiveness can alter film-removal and repair kinetics.
SEM/EDS can quantify passive-film thickness and defect density in the proposed experiment.
Failure of increasing sliding force to increase both wear rate and corrosion current density would falsify film-removal/repassivation competition as the governing mechanism.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says mechanical sliding disrupts the passive film, whereas the inert-sliding baseline is said to preserve that film. An inert atmosphere can suppress electrochemical corrosion but does not inherently prevent mechanical film removal.

Complete inhibition of repassivation is presented as a regime where the hypothesis may fail, although zero repair is the limiting case in which removal most clearly outpaces repair under the stated hypothesis.

The falsification rule requires both wear and corrosion current to rise with sliding force, but the hypothesis and uncertainty statement allow repassivation, microstructure, and environment to alter either response. Thus, a non-monotonic component could trigger the rule without disproving the proposed competition.
